title: His, her, their: the shared third-person ending
summary: His, her, and their use the same third-person possessive ending. With the back-vowel nouns pallo, kirja, and auto, that ending is -nsa.
objectives: Use the same noun ending for his, her, and their while keeping the owner clear.
Recognise the pattern, then produce it with the supporting words shown.

sections.title: How the pattern works
paragraphs: His, her, and their use the same third-person possessive ending. With the back-vowel nouns pallo, kirja, and auto, that ending is -nsa.

Hänen pallonsa means “his ball” or “her ball”; heidän pallonsa means “their ball”. The owner pronoun distinguishes one third-person owner from several; the noun ending alone does not. Keep the owner pronoun in these basic phrases.
keyPoints: His, her, their: the shared third-person ending
Practise one singular possessed thing with the supporting forms shown.

steps: Pallo (“ball”) + -nsa = pallonsa. Use this third-person ending for either gender.
Pallo (“ball”) + -nsa = pallonsa, exactly the same noun form as with hänen. The pronoun distinguishes the owners.
Choose hänen for a single third-person owner.
Auto (“car”) + -nsa = autonsa; changing the noun does not create a gender-specific ending.
Choose heidän for several third-person owners.
Kirja (“book”) + -nsa = kirjansa; keep the owner pronoun to express “their”.

commonMistakes: Hänen and heidän use the same noun ending: hänen pallonsa and heidän pallonsa. The pronoun distinguishes one owner from several.
Keep the owner pronoun in these phrases; pallonsa alone does not distinguish his/her from their.
Do not replace the shared third-person ending with a first- or second-person ending.
